title: General Concepts in Machine Learning
text:
Machine learning and “black boxes”

Linear and logistic regression:

We specify a mathematical relationship between the features and the response.
Model coefficients can often be interpreted directly.
Complex nonlinear relationships and interactions may be difficult to specify and interpret.




Machine learning models (e.g., random forests and neural networks):

Can learn complex, nonlinear relationships and interactions from data.
The fitted relationship between features and predictions is often difficult to interpret directly.
Often described as “black-box” models.

title: General Concepts in Machine Learning
text:
Machine learning and “black boxes”
EU’s Ethics guidelines for trustworthy AI (2019)
AI systems should respect ethical principles:

Human autonomy – humans should remain in control.
Prevention of harm – AI should not cause harm.
Fairness – avoid discrimination and unfair outcomes.
Explicability – decisions should be understandable and explainable.

Particular care is needed when AI affects vulnerable groups or when there are power imbalances (e.g., employers vs employees).
AI can bring substantial benefits, but also pose risks and have negative impacts that are difficult to predict or measure (e.g. on democracy, the rule of law, or on the human mind itself.)

title: General Concepts in Machine Learning

Feature importance: Global
Permutation importance

Idea: If a feature is important for the model, randomly shuffling its values should make the predictions worse.


Example:

Accuracy of recidivism model on test data: 78%
Randomly shuffle age in the test data: accuracy drops to 65%
Permutation importance of age: 78 - 65 = 13 percentage points



Caution: Correlated features complicate interpretation.

If age appears unimportant, it may be because other (unshuffled) features contain similar information.

Limited predictive stability: A single tree may not capture complex patterns reliably, especially when the data is noisy.

section: How do we estimate the parameters?
text:
How do we estimate the parameters?


We find the parameters that minimize the loss function: \[
\sum_{i =1 }^n(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2 = \sum_{i =1 }^n(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i-\dots)^2
\]
Note The model has strict assumption regarding parameters, linearity, independence

Model assumption and residuals
Remember: \(y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i\) where

\(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\) is the systematic part
\(\epsilon_i\) is the random error, with \(\epsilon_i \sim N(0,\sigma^2)\)

The key assumption we check with residuals is:
The errors should behave like (Gaussian) random noise.
A residual plot should therefore show:

Random scatter around 0
Roughly the same amount of spread across the range
No obvious curve or other pattern
No “funnel” shape

Course description

Content
Data science is about extracting knowledge from data. This includes identifying patterns, making predictions, communicating results, and supporting decision-making. This course provides a practical and example-based introduction to fundamental topics such as data visualisation, regression models, and machine learning. We will discuss the limitations of data analysis and modeling to avoid misinterpretation or misuse of model results.


Learning outcomes
The student is familiar with the most common methods and algorithms for data visualisation, modeling, and prediction. The student can critically evaluate results from various data science processes. This includes understanding the limitations of models, as well as being able to discuss the implications of these with others.


Learning and assessment activities
For this course your grade is set using portfolio assessment. You will attend and participate in mandatory activities, and complete (in groups) two projects. All activities and project work are intended to take place during the lecture times.

A t-test
A two-sample t-test asks:

Is the difference between the two group means large relative to the variation within the groups?

\[
H_0:\mu_{\text{no phone}}=\mu_{\text{phone}}
\qquad\text{vs}\qquad
H_A:\mu_{\text{no phone}}<\mu_{\text{phone}}
\]


t = -4.14

title: Linear Regression
text:
But are the groups comparable?
Imagine that the two groups differ in more ways than just owning a phone.
For example: Parent’s years of education
Brief group discussion: Why might this matter?


It may be that high and low educated parents have different patterns when it comes to buying phones
It may also be the parents education has something to say for the children’s sleeping patterns

title: Linear Regression
text:
A potential confounder
Let’s look at parent education and mobile ownership

title: Linear Regression
text:
A potential confounder
Let’s look at parent education and sleep.

title: Linear Regression
text:
Confounding: the key idea
A confounder is a variable that is related to:

the thing we are comparing, and
the outcome we care about.

Parent education interacts with both mobile ownership and sleep
So the mobile/no-mobile comparison can mix together several differences.

title: Linear Regression
text:
So what can we do?
We would like to make a fairer comparison.
Instead of asking:

“How different is sleep between children with and without mobiles?”

we can ask:

“How different is sleep between children with and without mobiles, after accounting for parent education?”

Short group discussion: What does after accounting for parent education means?

title: Linear Regression
text:
Regression
Regression allows us to describe the outcome using several variables.
For example:
Sleep = mobile ownership + parent education + other variation
The important idea is:

Each coefficient describes the relationship between a predictor and the outcome while taking the other predictors into account.

title: Linear Regression
text:
Simple linear regression
A linear regression with only mobile ownership is essentially a group comparison.
\[
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i
\]

\(y_i\) hours of sleep for child \(i\)
\(x_i\) mobile ownership (0/1) for child \(i\)
\(\beta_0, \beta_1\) coefficient to be estimated
\(\epsilon_i\) this is the “error” that we assume is independent and identical distributed among all observations

Short group discussion: Do you remember what independent and identical distributed means?

title: Linear Regression
text:
Simple linear regression - Fitted model


\[
\widehat{Sleep}
=
7.77
-0.28\times Mobile
\]




Interpretation

\(\beta_0\) Average over the whole group: on average the group of children sleeps 7.77 hours per night
\(\beta_1\) Difference between not owning and owning a mobile decreases the hours of sleep by 0.28
Testing for \(\beta_1 = 0\) is equivalent to the t-test we had before!

title: Linear Regression
text:
Adding a potential confounder
A linear regression with only mobile ownership is essentially a group comparison.
\[
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \beta_2 x_{2i} + \epsilon_i
\]

\(y_i\) hours of sleep for child \(i\)
\(x_{1i}\) mobile ownership (0/1) for child \(i\)
\(x_{2i}\) years of parents education for child \(i\)
\(\beta_0, \beta_1, \beta_2\) are model parameters

title: Linear Regression
text:
The fitted model


\[
\widehat{Sleep}
=
6.22
-0.58\times Mobile
+0.14\times ParentEducation
\]




Interpretation

\(\hat{\beta_0} = 6.22\) The predicted sleep when Mobile = 0 and ParentEducation = 0.
\(\hat{\beta_1} = −0.58\) children with a mobile are predicted to sleep 0.50 hours less per night than those without a mobile, holding constant the parents years of education.
\(\beta_2=0.12\) each additional year of parent education is associated with 0.12 additional hours of predicted sleep, holding constant the mobile ownership.

title: Linear Regression
text:
What does “holding constant” mean?
Suppose we compare two children who are similar with respect to parent education:

both have parents with 14 years of education
one child has a mobile
one child does not

Regression asks about the expected difference in their sleep
The mobile coefficient is a comparison after accounting for parent education.

title: Linear Regression
text:
Comparing the models
Let’s compare the estimated coefficients for mobile ownership in the two models:


Simple linear regression estimate:      -0.28 hours
Adjusted estimated: -0.58 hours


The estimates are different because mobile ownership and parent education are related in our simulated data.

title: Linear Regression
section: What can regression do and what it cannot
text:
What can regression do and what it cannot
Regression can adjust for variables that:

we have measured, and
we have included in the model.

It cannot automatically fix:

an important confounder we did not measure
poor measurement
a badly specified model
selection problems

title: Linear Regression
text:
How about causality?

Adjustment does not prove causation.

A safer phrase is:
“association after adjustment”
unless the study design and assumptions justify a causal interpretation.

title: Linear Regression
text:
Take-home message
Linear regression is a way to compare and explain relationships

Simple regression with a binary predictor is essentially a comparison of two group means.
Multiple regression lets us compare groups while accounting for other variables.
Each coefficient describes the association between a predictor and the outcome holding the other predictors constant.
A coefficient tells us how much the predicted outcome changes for a one-unit change in the predictor.
Regression does not automatically imply causation. Adjustment can reduce confounding, but it does not guarantee a causal interpretation.


Regression lets us make more informative comparisons by considering several variables at the same time.

Take home messages from today

Different models make different assumptions about the data.
Too simple models may underfit and very flexible models may overfit.
We want models that generalize well to new observations.
Model parameters (such as \(k\) in k-NN) can be tuned using cross-validation.
Our goal is not to fit the training data perfectly but to make accurate predictions on data we have not seen before.

title: Neural networks and multiclass prediction
text:
Multiclass prediction
How do we go from a list of probabilities to an actual prediction?
Decision rule for us today:
\[
\widehat{y} = \arg\max_{k \in \{0,\ldots,9\}} \widehat{p}_k
\]

title: Neural networks and multiclass prediction
text:
Multiclass prediction
What is a good prediction method?

Accuracy of predictions on test data:
\[
\text{accuracy} = \frac{\text{number of correct predictions}}{\text{total number of predictions}}
\]


But in the model building phase (training data) we will work with minimizing some loss function.

title: Neural networks and multiclass prediction
text:
Multiclass prediction
What is a good prediction method?
Loss function for us today: cross-entropy

Example: If the true digit is \(y = 3\) then the loss is:
\[
L = -\log (\widehat{p}_3)
\]


This loss function rewards putting high probability on the true class.


For example, for \(y = 3\):
If \(\widehat{p}_3 = 0.9\) then \(L \approx 0.1\)
If \(\widehat{p}_3 = 0.3\) then \(L \approx 1.2\)

title: Neural networks and multiclass prediction
text:
Neural networks: Gradient descent
To find the parameter values that minimize the loss over the training data we want to know which direction to change each parameter to reduce the loss.

Gradient descent (very informally!):

Current parameters: Make predictions and calculate loss
Check: How would changing each parameter affect the loss?
Update/change parameters in a direction that lowers the loss
Repeat



Backpropagation is the procedure neural networks use to work out how the parameters contributed to the loss.


Stopping criterion: When should we stop updating parameters?

When we have reached a maximum number of iterations
When the loss is no longer improving substantially
…

Neural networks: Hyperparameter tuning
For our specified network:

1 hidden layer,
32 hidden nodes,
ReLU activation,
etc,

we use training data to estimate 25 450 unknown parameters (weights and biases).

But why 1 hidden layer, 32 nodes and ReLU? These are hyperparameters, and we might want to consider other choices (“architectures”).


For each architecture, we train the network using the training data.
Then using validation data, (or cross-validation) we compare the trained models and make choices.
